nameStory: The night-flowering catchfly gets its name from two key behaviors: its white flowers open in the evening and stay open through the night to attract nocturnal pollinators like moths. The 'catchfly' part comes from its sticky stems that can trap small insects, though this isn't its main method of getting food like true carnivorous plants.
description: Night-flowering catchfly is a weedy annual plant that grows 1-3 feet tall with sticky, hairy stems and leaves. It produces small white flowers that open at dusk and close during the day, giving it a rather unremarkable appearance unless you catch it at the right time. This European native has made itself at home in disturbed soils across much of North America, often popping up in farm fields, roadsides, and waste areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers that open in evening and close by morning, with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost divided in half; flowers have a sweet, light fragrance most noticeable at night

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sticky, clammy stems covered in fine hairs that will make your fingers feel tacky when you touch them; often trap small insects and debris

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are lance-shaped and also sticky to the touch, with prominent veins and a slightly fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant typically 1-3 feet tall with branching stems, often growing in patches in disturbed ground

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small egg-shaped capsules that split open to release tiny dark seeds, often with dried flower parts still attached at the tip

habitat: Look for night-flowering catchfly in disturbed soils like farm fields, roadsides, vacant lots, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in areas where the soil has been turned over or compacted, and doesn't compete well in established natural areas. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy plants in agricultural settings or along paths and driveways.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, producing small rosettes of sticky leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from mid-summer through early fall, with the distinctive evening-opening white flowers most visible at dusk and dawn. Peak blooming time is July and August.
seasonality.fall: Late-season flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed capsule formation and dispersal before first frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts survive winter, but seeds remain dormant in the soil until spring warmth triggers germination.

funFact: This plant is essentially a night owl of the flower world - its blooms open like clockwork at dusk and close by mid-morning, meaning most people walk right past it during the day without ever seeing its flowers open!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with white campion, but white campion has larger, showier flowers and lacks the extremely sticky, clammy feel of night-flowering catchfly's stems and leaves. Memory trick: if touching the plant makes your fingers feel like you stuck them in honey, it's night-flowering catchfly.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'clammy cockle' in some regions, this plant isn't related to the cockles you might find at the beach - that's just an old term for plants with similar-looking seed capsules. The stickiness that traps insects isn't for carnivorous purposes but likely helps protect the plant from crawling pests that might damage it.
compareHints: Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule. White campion has similar white flowers but opens during the day and lacks the tacky feel, while bladder campion has inflated, balloon-like flower bases that night-flowering catchfly doesn't have. Most other catchflies in New England have pink or red flowers rather than white.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
